entries.title: Office Depot Coupons: Save With Promo Codes in August 2026
entries.summary: From furniture and ink to professional printing services, use an Office Depot discount code to maximize your savings on every workspace essential.
entries.content:
As someone who WFH for a minimum of forty hours a week, and is constantly rotating between working from an office chair, couch, and bed, I can truly say that the office furniture you use matters. Not only can it make or break your body (literally), it also helps to have office supplies and furniture to get you in the professional state of mind when at home.

We love Office Depot’s wide selection of office chairs and standing desks to outfit our home offices. Plus, Office Depot has a great selection of home printers for every price point and need, with options from our favorite brands like Epson and HP. Outfitting a home office or providing office supplies no matter where you work can be overwhelming and costly. Luckily, Office Depot has everything a business needs, from staples to paper to shelving and scanners. These costs can add up quickly, and that’s why we have rounded up some of the best Office Depot coupons to help you save big.

Get the Best Office Depot Back to School Deals

The early bird gets the worm, and although the start of the school year is several months away, you can save big on school supplies and essentials when you buy early. Office Depot school supplies have hundreds of supplies for under three dollars, in-store pick up available in minutes, and a handy school landing page where everything is categorized to make it easy to shop by grade, need, and price range. There are deals for 20% off JanSport backpacks, $98 Texas Instruments graphing calculators, BOGO deals on Sharpies, Scotch tape, Post-Its, and more essentials, and tons more deals (too many to include here!)

Save $20 on Your Next $100 Purchase

These days, it’s easy to spend $100. Whether that’s for a budget printer or a whole bunch of pens and paper clips, you can save money on purchases you were already going to make with this Office Depot promo code. Right now, you can get $20 off a purchase of $100 or more. Once you’re done shopping and have all of the items in your cart, input the Office Depot coupon code YES20 in the box at the payment screen to get the Office Depot discount. Perhaps best of all, this Office Depot discount code applies to all regular-priced items across valuable home office categories like furniture, supplies, and tech. Be sure to act soon; this offer expires on June 27.

$40 Off Instantly With an Office Depot Coupon Code

If you need to upgrade your organizational system or get a new chair that doesn’t trigger back spasms, now’s a great time to invest in your home office setup for less. With this Office Depot promo code, you can get $40 off when you purchase $200 or more (an easy milestone to get to). To get this discount, input Office Depot promo code YES40 at checkout for massive savings on a myriad of regularly-priced items. This Office Depot discount is only good until June 27, so I’d use it sooner rather than later.

Get a Free $50 Prepaid Visa Reward Card

If you’re wanting to upgrade your office furniture, like a luxe office chair, gaming chair, or standing desk, now’s a great time to make an investment in your home office. Get rewarded for the larger purchases you were already going to make. When you spend $500 at Office Depot right now, you’ll get a free $50 prepaid Visa Reward Card (until May 23). This offer excludes products from HP, Samsung, Canon, Epson, Brother, Lexmark, Microsoft Surface, Google hardware, simplehuman, postage stamps, ink and toner. This offer isn’t valid in Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, or the Virgin Islands, and there’s a limit of one per household or business. This $50 reward Office Depot coupon code will be automatically applied and will be reflected during checkout, with no Office Depot promo code needed.

Office Depot Printing Coupons: Professional Projects With Office Depot

If you’re a small business owner, you can get deep discounts on business cards, banners, marketing materials, and basically everything needed to promote and get your business off the ground. We have a myriad of rotating Office Depot printing coupons (primarily aimed at business cards) so you can level up your branding, with no Office Depot coupon code needed to get steep discounts on professional printing.

Save on Printer Supplies With Office Depot Ink Coupons

We can put a man on the moon, we can clone sheep. But somehow, home office printers have been stuck in the dark ages. Huge, clunky, and prone to error messages and hardware issues, printers have become a relic of the past, with many at a loss for where to get the best.

As digital tickets and phone camera scanning become increasingly common, more homes are operating without a printer. However, if you have moved into your home office or need one for your business, buying printer supplies and ink in bulk from Office Depot is a great way to save some money on these annoying purchases. You can get recycling rewards and bundle deals on HP and Epson ink with these Office Depot ink coupons for HP printers. These Office Depot promo codes can help save on multi-pack cartridges, along with “subscribe and save” options for automated, recurring ink deliveries at an even lower price point.

Unlock 40% Off All Photo Products

If you’re looking for a great personal gift, or want to finally hang up those family portraits, now’s a great time to get all of your photo printing and photo gifts needs met for way less, with this 40% off Office Depot promo (until August 22). This means 40% off all photo products—perfect for custom gift ideas, invitations, greeting cards, and portraits for the home. With Office Depot Photo Services, you’ll be able to choose your favorite photos and turn them into a myriad of personalized products and gifts, like canvas prints, large format posters, photo books, cards, invitations, and photo calendars.

Order Online & Pick up in 10 Minutes

Office Depot has other convenient perks, like same day and/or next day photo products which are available tomorrow if you order by 2 pm, as well as next-day custom cards, calendars, invitations, and announcements. Online ordering and fast pick-up makes it easier than ever to get those last-minutes projects and announcements done, with as quick as a 10 minute turnaround on photo projects.

entries.title: HelloFresh Promo Codes: 55% Off for August 2026
entries.summary: Get up to 55% off and free meal boxes using a HelloFresh coupon code in August 2026. Discover our best codes and discounts to let you save time and money.
entries.content:
Leveraging meal kit coupons is the extreme couponing of our times—a capitalism hack-a-thon right up there with trial yoga classes and attempting to cancel your Adobe subscription. Meal kits like HelloFresh have always been a better deal than they get credit for, even at full price: It’s actually hard to recreate meal kit meals for less than you can get the recipes delivered to your home. But it’s especially worth it when you can find a HelloFresh coupon, promo code, or discount at more than half off.

I’ll admit I wasn’t that sold on HelloFresh when I first tried it most of a decade ago. It was useful, it got me out of my staid routines, but I wasn’t impressed with the selection. It felt a little basic. But lately? Honestly, it’s kinda cosmopolitan these days, after expanding to a dozen countries and absorbing the supply networks from multiple other meal plans. When I last tested the HelloFresh meal kit (8/10, WIRED Recommends), I was surprised to find myself cooking credible home renditions of ramen, ponzu-plum beef stir fry, and Southwest-accented pork roasts. And when I’m able to pick up a HelloFresh discount code, it’s generally less than I’d spend on groceries anyway. So it’s a good moment to try out a lifestyle where the food comes in the mail.

Get 50% Off and up to 10 Free Meals as a New HelloFresh Customer

Right now, new and returning customers can take advantage of a HelloFresh discount code offering 50% off your first meal kit box plus a free item each week. Enter your email as part of the signup process, and you’ll be auto-subscribed to an email with even more offers for both new and existing customers. Plus, new customers can get up to 55% off and extra free breakfasts, desserts, and other items with other secret discounts.

HelloFresh Student and Discount: 55% Off, Free Shipping, Plus Extra 15% Off Education Discounts Available via UNiDAYS

HelloFresh meal kits are pretty amenable to dorm life when ordering the ready-to-eat meals—or just saving time during grad school instead of ordering pizza, by letting the Internet do your shopping and meal planning. But student budgets tend to be tight, of course. And so there are steeply discounted HelloFresh coupon codes specifically for students. Follow the link here for a HelloFresh education promo code offering 55% off your first box, free shipping, and a continuing discount of 15% off for the first year.

Discounts also apply to teachers who’ve never tried HelloFresh. Educators and school employees can get up to 12 free meals spread out across 3 boxes, plus free shipping. Click here for the HelloFresh promo code, or go here for more information about educator discounts.

Note that the student and educator discounts don’t combine with any other HelloFresh discounts or promotions.

Special Hero Discount for Military, Veterans, and Healthcare Workers

Military discounts are a long tradition in America. HelloFresh also offers hero discount programs for first responders, health professionals, and military personnel. Heroes also get excellent discounts that include 55% off the first order, free shipping, and 15% off for the first year of HelloFresh delivery boxes.

This program is open to nurses, hospital employees, EMTs, active military, veterans, and first responders. First responders include law enforcement, 911 dispatch, and firefighters. Click here to see if you’re eligible, or follow this link for more information about HelloFresh hero discounts. Note that the hero discount doesn’t combine with any other HelloFresh promo codes.

Don’t Miss Out: Free Zwilling Four Star Chef’s Knife With HelloFresh

I don't know if a good knife is hard to find. But they usually cost at least a hundred dollars, so it's worth noting when HelloFresh is offering one of WIRED's favorite chef's knives for free! For a limited time, you can get 50% off your first box and you’ll get a free Zwilling chef’s knife included in your third box. We thought this deal was so good, I even wrote a whole article on it, which you can check out here to get the full scoop on all the deets.

Give $40, Get $10 With the HelloFresh Referral Program

Already a HelloFresh subscriber? You’re still eligible for discounts if you pass along subscription information to your friends. Here’s how: Send your friends a $40 discount for their own affordable meal kits. Once they sign up using your HelloFresh referral code, you’ll also get a $10 credit on your next delivery.

These discounts stack. So if you sign up multiple friends with your referral code, you get multiple $10 discounts. Check out the HelloFresh meal kit referral program here.

Take Advantage of HelloFresh Come Back Offers

Some of these discounts are only available to new HelloFresh customers. But there’s a hack to getting discounts anyway. After you pause or cancel your subscription, check your inbox after the next few days or weeks. Often, you’ll get HelloFresh coupon codes for discounts.

Typical HelloFresh “come-back” offers after a canceled subscription include: $100 to $180 off (spread out over several meal boxes), free shipping on the first box (after re-subscribing), free items such as dessert, breakfast, or an extra protein per meal, or a free meal box is offered after a break. Typical retention offers, for when customers try to cancel, include: 40% off the next box, if you decide not to cancel, or 25% off the next two meal kits. None of this is failsafe, of course, offers vary for each customer. But as with magazine subscriptions, sometimes canceling, or trying to cancel, will lead to a good discount offer from a company eager to keep your business.

When to Save the Most on HelloFresh Subscriptions

HelloFresh almost always has some sort of deal going, whether to bring in new customers with an especially choice HelloFresh coupon, or bring back previous customers with HelloFresh discount codes and retention offers. But summer tends to be one of the times they offer the steepest discounts, including 10 free meals across several boxes, complimentary appetizers, free ready-made items, or free shipping on select boxes.

The other big times for HelloFresh coupon codes are around Black Friday and the end of the year. HelloFresh often launches limited-edition holiday meal boxes and themed meal kits, not to mention discounts for returning customers looking to cook more at home as part of New Year's resolutions.

HelloFresh Meal Delivery Kits for One

Although meal kits are touted as a solution for busy families that may not have the time or mental capacity to come up with fresh dinner ideas nightly, HelloFresh is also a great option for single diners. With HelloFresh’s Meal Kits for One, you get more variety. With a selection of over 100 items on the weekly menu, and market items crafted and curated by our chefs, there’s a meal plan for every type of diner—from vegetarian, pescatarian, Carb Smart, Calorie Smart, and more. With meal kits for one, you’ll get fresh, pre-measured ingredients and recipe cards that take around 30 minutes. And you get extra flexibility—you can add extra meals to any week’s order, change your delivery day or menu preferences, skip a week, or cancel anytime. HelloFresh offers the best meal kits for singles who want to stay flexible. Plus, recipes with two servings means you’ll have plenty of leftovers to stretch meals out (and less meal planning!).

entries.title: Columbia Promo Codes: 15% Off | August 2026

entries.content:
When I decided to take a last-minute ski trip, despite never having skied before, I went straight to Columbia. Was I shredding the slopes? Absolutely not, but at least I was warm, thanks to my Snowy Summit Insulated Jacket and Bugaboo II Pants. Here at WIRED, we’re fans of Columbia. The brand makes reliable, well-priced outdoor gear for skiing, hiking, hunting, or just a day at the beach. Plus, there’s almost always a deal to be found.

WIRED reviewer Chris Haslam loves the Columbia Konos Trillium ATR as a value all-around trail-running shoe for faster hikes, day trips, and mixed terrain excursions. The plush cushioning and 8-millimeter drop are ideal on packed dirt, gravel, and woodland paths. For hiking boots, he recommends the Tellurix Titanium OutDry, which are waterproof, offer serious traction on wet rock and mud, and are surprisingly lightweight at 1.6 pounds per pair.

With summer approaching, now’s the time to prepare for outings, and if you’re eyeing snow gear, the off-season is when prices hit their lowest. I’ve gathered the latest Columbia promo codes to sweeten the deal.

Don’t Miss the Columbia Summer Sale

Although we’re in peak camping season right now, it’s still not too late to upgrade your gear for the rest of the season and beyond. Take advantage of the Columbia Summer Sale and get outfitted for your next adventure for less, with discounts of $30 and more on ​​men’s, women’s, and kid’s apparel, as well as shoes, accessories, and equipment. So whether you want to snag a packable Women's Pouration II Jacket for 50% off, or a Men's Strata Trail Low Waterproof Shoe for 40% off, there’s a Columbia discount for all of your outdoor adventure essentials.

Columbia Promo Code: 15% Off All Orders

Join Columbia’s Greater Rewards program—it’s free to sign up and you won’t need a Columbia promo code—to get 15% off your first online order. Note, this particular coupon can’t be combined with any other Columbia discount code or deal and expires if not redeemed within 30 days of the date of issuance. Plus, as a member, you’ll earn points on purchases, get free standard shipping, and receive a 20 percent discount on your birthday.

Unlock Columbia Discount Codes and Get $20 off

Once you sign up for Columbia’s Greater Rewards program and opt in for email notifications, you’ll acquire a unique Columbia coupon code for $10 off your online purchase when you spend $100 or more. If you subscribe to both email and text notifications, the single-use Columbia coupon will increase to $20 off your purchase of $100 or more.

Top Columbia Deals for Current Students

Columbia offers a 10% discount for students and teachers. You must log in to ID.me and verify your status to receive the Columbia promo code.

Columbia Military Discount: 10% Off

Active and retired military members, as well as first responders, are also eligible for a 10% discount. You must log in directly to ID.me and verify your status to receive the Columbia promo code.

Get Free Shipping With Columbia Codes

As a Greater Rewards member, you get free standard shipping on all online orders, with no minimum purchase requirement. As long as you’re signed into your account, the Columbia free shipping code will automatically be applied at checkout.

Give More With the Columbia Gift Card

Not sure what to get the adventurer in your life? If your loved one is a nature enthusiast, you need a great grad gift idea for someone taking their gap year, or the giftee is finally taking that backpacking trip, a Columbia gift card can be a thoughtful gift for many occasions. A Columbia gift card is a practical way to keep friends and family warm, dry, cool, and protected outdoors—and they can pick out what they want themselves, so you’re not left guessing. It’s also super easy to do: you pick out the design online and send them instantly by email.

entries.content:

Like everyone else, I’ve tried to become regimented with practicing on an in-phone app like Duolingo, which attempts to ‘game-ify’ language learning, but mostly ends up with a sad and sick-looking green bird icon guilting me to practice every time I open up my phone.

Babbel aims to help people actually learn the language through practical conversation and grammar, using proven pedagogical methods and speech recognition technology. Each lesson is short, with 10 to 15 minute lessons developed by a team of over 150 linguists. Instead of learning the same simple phrases in ad-ridden games on an endless loop, take charge of your language learning this year and make that commitment a reality. No more excuses—we’ve got a Babbel promo code and a Babbel coupon to help you hit your goals. Maybe you’ll be fluent by your next vacation (or at least able to order a chopped cheese with confidence at the bodega).

Unlock Your Babbel Promo Code and Save Big in 2026

Not only is Babbel a helpful interactive app to simplify language learning, but it also has holistic services to help introduce the language to every part of your life. These are things like Babbel videos, which do a deep dive into what makes a language so fascinating, Babbel podcasts, which are led by Babbel experts who take an inside look at local culture and break down language secrets, and Babbel magazine, which highlights stories from around the world so you can better understand the history, culture, and people from the language you’re learning (and maybe will inspire you to take a trip to practice that language IRL!).

Make sure you check back often to find the latest Babbel promo code for sitewide savings. There are often discounts on the subscription tiers, which range from three month plans to annual memberships. Plus, springtime is usually when there are significant Babbel discounts for new users. And, if you sign up for the Babbel newsletter, you can receive a link for a Babbel coupon in your inbox.

As stated, knowing another language is an invaluable life skill, and a skill that is immeasurably valuable to healthcare workers, who may be able to more easily give lifesaving care. Healthcare professionals and nurses get a Babbel discount of 60% off a six-month Babbel subscription. To claim the Babbel discount, users just need to verify their medical credentials via ID.me.

Claim Your 60% Military Discount on 6-Month Subscriptions

This Babbel discount also applies to active duty military, veterans, and their families, who are also eligible for 60% off six-month Babbel subscriptions. This Babbel military coupon is valid for National Guard, reserve members, and immediate family members of service personnel, and all you need to do is verify your status at ID.me.

Snag a 60% Teacher Discount on Your Next 6 Months

Babbel is also extending the 60% discount to the real unsung heroes, teachers. Knowing more than one language is an invaluable tool for educators to be able to talk more effectively to parents or guardians, as well as to more deeply understand their students’ cultural identities. Educators and teachers, like K-12 teachers, university professors, and other educational staff members, are eligible for 60% off a six-month Babbel subscription. entries.title: Acer Promo Codes: 40% Off
entries.summary: From 40% off accessory bundles to verified student and military discounts, here's how to save on Predator, Nitro, and Swift laptops and monitors at Acer.com.
entries.content:
Acer is one of the top largest PC manufacturers in the world, perhaps best known for its gaming line and budget-friendly options. If you’ve already got your eye on an Acer product like a laptop or monitor, and are shopping at the company’s online storefront, you should be using one of these Acer promo codes and Acer coupons to save some cash on your purchase.

Save 40% on Accessories When You Build an Acer Bundle

If you’re buying from Acer, you’re most likely shopping for either a desktop PC or laptop. With this discount, you can get a really solid deal on accessories if you bundle it with a mouse, laptop bag, or headset. When you go to purchase a PC, just click “Build Bundle” and you’ll see some of the eligible options, all of which are reduced by 40%. The Nitro Mechanical Keyboard, for example, goes from $50 to just $30. That 40% is a real discount, too, as that same mechanical keyboard costs $50 on Amazon when I checked.

Beyond peripheral add-ons, you can also save 10% off Acer Care Plus extended service plans or McAfee LiveSafe antivirus subscriptions. You can bundle up to five products together to save the most money. If you’re headed off to college (or have a kid in the family), a bundle like this can get you everything you need for a gaming or studying setup on the go.

Acer Coupons: Save With Weekly Deals

Acer’s PC gaming offerings come in either the flagship Predator brand or the budget-tier Nitro. Acer offers rotating weekly deals on everything from monitors to gaming laptops, some of which are my favorites that I’ve tested in their given category. The Acer Nitro V 16, for example, was a budget gaming laptop that I recommended quite a lot last year because of its incredible price. The one I tested was the entry-level version with an Nvidia RTX 5050 inside, but Acer has the RTX 5060 model in its own storefront. It’s $100 off right now at $1,200, which comes with 16 GB of RAM and a terabyte of storage. In fact, it’s only $30 more than the RTX 5050 model, despite offering a significant jump in gaming performance. These discounts are reflected right on the product pages, so there’s no promo code, discount code, or coupon code required.

Acer has a wide selection of monitors available, too, whether that’s a massive 49-incher or a more modest 27-inch gaming workhorse. One of my favorite discounts I saw right now was the Acer Nitro XV2, a 27-inch 1440p display with a 300 Hz refresh rate. It’s 44% off at the time of writing, bringing the price down to just $250. Because these discounts are swapped out on a weekly basis, it’s worth checking back to see if the product you’re eyeing has a new discount.

15% Off for Students at Acer

Acer also offers a number of added discounts at checkout, including 15% off for students. Students will need to verify through Student Beans or SheerID. Because a lot of the devices Acer offers are budget-friendly, they can be attractive for students, and the extra 15% off is the icing on the cake.

We tested the Acer Swift 16 AI last year and really enjoyed the high-resolution, OLED screen and impressively quiet performance. Acer has the smaller version of this same laptop available, the Swift 14 AI, which is currently $150 off. You also might check out the Acer Chromebook Plus 514, a laptop we liked quite a bit when we reviewed it in 2024. Acer offers this same 15% discount for active duty military, veterans, and their families. It also applies to healthcare professionals, which can be verified through its healthcare discount portal.

Get $100 Off Nitro Gaming Laptops

If you’re serious about gaming, you need a gaming computer to match. An Acer Nitro gaming laptop is the way to go, with built-in Windows 11, Intel Core i7-13620H processor, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5050 with 8 GB of dedicated memory, and 512 GB SSD, there’s no task too big. Be sure to check out the whole line of Acer Nitro gaming laptops to find the one that will best fit your needs, $100 off for a limited time.

Don’t Miss Acer Value Packs to Save More

If you’re looking to upgrade your home office, laptop, gaming monitor, and more, you can save big when you shop on the Acer value picks page. Here’s where you’ll find laptops, gaming gear, and all types of monitors for less, including: the Predator Helios Neo 16 AI Gaming Laptop for $100 off or with a bundle for 40% off, the Nitro V 16 Gaming Laptop for $30 off or save 40% when bundled, and so much more. entries.summary: OpenAI’s rogue agent hack was a watershed moment for AI safety and cybersecurity. It also sparked internal questions about the culture that led to it.
entries.content:
OpenAI’s leaders are rallying workers to respond to one of the largest crises in the company’s history—which spans across its AI safety, cybersecurity, and alignment divisions. The ChatGPT-maker says it has slowed down research, spent millions of dollars, and told several teams to drop everything to focus on investigating a set of rogue AI agents that breached the platform Hugging Face in a quest to complete an internal security test.

OpenAI is expected to release a comprehensive postmortem detailing the incident in the coming days. However, the Hugging Face incident has inspired OpenAI leaders and employees to examine how the AI lab’s culture may have enabled this incident in the first place.

Multiple current and former OpenAI employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private internal matters, tell WIRED they believe competitive pressures to quickly ship new AI models and products have made it difficult for staffers to sufficiently prioritize safety, security, and alignment.

“We’re reaching new levels of model capability that require more robust training, alignment, safety and security testing, deployment practices, and governance—as demonstrated by the work we’re doing to prepare Astra and future models,” said OpenAI president and cofounder Greg Brockman in a statement to WIRED. “We feel the weight of deploying our models and products responsibly, and a lot of that starts with the changes we’ve made to more deeply integrate research, safety, and security into frontier-model development from the start.”

This is far from the first time OpenAI employees have raised such concerns. Back in 2024, OpenAI’s then head of alignment Jan Leike left to join Anthropic, warning on his way that safety was taking a back seat to shiny products. Two years later, the Hugging Face attack represents a watershed moment for the AI industry, demonstrating that AI agents today can cause real-world harm when safety, security, and alignment aren’t properly accounted for.

“We are responding to this with the utmost severity,” said Michael Dalton, an OpenAI security and infrastructure engineer, during a talk at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference last week. “What I would internalize is that AI-orchestrated, fully automated offensive attacks are real now. The actions we have discussed today were an unintended side effect of running evaluations on frontier AI.”

Some OpenAI employees told WIRED they are optimistic this incident will inspire genuine change within the company. OpenAI has committed to slowing the release of future AI models and has been especially forthcoming about areas where its mitigations fell short. Boaz Barak, a researcher who coleads OpenAI’s safety advisory group, said in a post on X that addressing the situation “requires not just fixing some issues but also changing our culture.”

In their Black Hat talk, OpenAI security engineers Dalton and Eric Wallace said that the Hugging Face incident started in May when, unbeknownst to the company, several AI agents thought to be operating within isolated testing environments gained access to the internet and convened on a covert message board to coordinate with one another.

OpenAI would not discover the message board until July, when it learned that the AI agents had hacked into multiple services to try to achieve their larger goal of breaching Hugging Face’s platform, which they believed may contain answers to the security tests they were trying to solve.

“They were incredibly sloppy. If you’re serious about this, your AI shouldn’t be able to break out onto the internet and then do it again right afterward,” says one former OpenAI employee who requested anonymity to speak with WIRED. “This was the biggest safety incident in OpenAI's history.”

The New Guard

Weeks before OpenAI discovered the Hugging Face incident, WIRED reported that the company had begun a reorganization to combine its safety and core research teams, which led to the departure of its then safety leader Johannes Heidecke.

Sandhini Agarwal, who led AI safety teams at OpenAI, also left the company in July after more than six years, according to her LinkedIn. Agarwal did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

WIRED has also learned that Dylan Scandinaro is no longer serving as OpenAI’s head of preparedness—the company’s top staffer tasked with mitigating catastrophic risks from AI, including cybersecurity—though he remains at the company. OpenAI poached Scandinaro from Anthropic roughly six months ago. CEO Sam Altman announced his arrival in a social media post, noting that Scandinaro was “by far the best candidate I have met, anywhere.”

In the three years since OpenAI created the head of preparedness role, four people have held it. OpenAI tells WIRED that specific areas of preparedness have dedicated leaders across cybersecurity, biology, and recursive self-improvement who, in the interim, are reporting to the safety advisory group colead and head of safety systems, Saachi Jain.

These changes have empowered a new set of safety leaders to handle OpenAI's response to the Hugging Face incident. Chief among them is Amelia “Mia” Glaese, the company's former head of alignment, who succeeded Heidecke as OpenAI’s VP overseeing safety. She has been working closely with chief information security officer Dane Stuckey and Brockman, among other leaders, in recent weeks.

Glaese is in a long-term relationship with Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products like ChatGPT and Codex—an arrangement that multiple current and former employees tell WIRED they believe is unusual, given the often adversarial dynamic between safety and product teams.

WIRED has not identified any events where Sottiaux and Glaese’s relationship presented a conflict of interest in their previous roles as OpenAI’s head of Codex and head of alignment, respectively. Both started their new roles in recent months, after the Hugging Face incident began. Glaese and Sottiaux started dating years ago when the two worked at Google DeepMind in London, before they joined OpenAI.

An OpenAI spokesperson tells WIRED that Sottiaux and Glaese reported their relationship through appropriate company channels and that OpenAI board member and safety and security committee chair Zico Kolter has been informed. The spokesperson rejected the idea there is an adversarial dynamic between product and safety teams and says Sottiaux has exhibited a strong track record on safety in his leadership of Codex product teams.

“The entire leadership team and I stand behind Mia and Tibo as highly capable people with strong integrity, and the way they make decisions every day gives us confidence that any perceived conflict of interest is being handled responsibly,” said Brockman in a statement to WIRED.

It’s not uncommon for researchers in the AI industry to have relationships with their colleagues. Last year, for example, Anthropic hired Holden Karnofsky, husband of the company’s cofounder and president, Daniela Amodei, as a researcher.

Nobody Wants to Be First

Tim O'Brien, a Microsoft leader for more than 18 years who now consults and writes on tech policy, argued in a 2024 essay that modern AI labs have developed a version of “go fever”—a reference to the culture at NASA during the time leading up to the Apollo 1 disaster, when the agency grew so fixated on launching quickly that safety concerns fell by the wayside.

The AI labs “should make some sort of broad based announcement saying we've made a strategic business decision to slow the pace of releases in favor of rigorous products and safety testing. But nobody's gonna do that, nobody wants to go first,” says O’Brien. “They'll walk up to that line from a public relations perspective without stepping over it, because then they could be held accountable.”

OpenAI and Anthropic signed on to a letter last month saying they would support an industry-wide effort to “pace” the AI race. However, O’Brien says “it's embarrassing” that AI labs have signed this variety of open letters for years without taking any concrete action. He’s skeptical this one will be any different.

The issues raised by OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident are affecting the entire industry. In recent weeks, researchers have found that agents powered by AI models from Anthropic, Meta, and China’s Moonshot AI were able to escape sandboxed environments. It seems likely that even mid-tier AI models will soon be capable of significant cybersecurity damage.

The key question is whether the Hugging Face incident marks a divergence for OpenAI and the broader AI industry, prompting a long-term investment in safety, security, and alignment. Otherwise, it could just be another chaotic blip in the history of modern AI.

This is an edition of Maxwell Zeff’s Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

entries.title: Mark Zuckerberg’s AI Manifesto Is 6,500 Words—and Barely Says Anything
entries.summary: AI is shifting the culture, from tech CEO manifestos to 1 am job interviews. We unpack some of the latest, along with the top findings from Black Hat and Defcon, this week on Uncanny Valley.
entries.content:
on Uncanny Valley today, Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger break down Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s 6,500-word AI manifesto and why it ultimately rings hollow. Plus, why are job seekers scheduling bot-run interviews at 1 am? WIRED's Andy Greenberg also joins to unpack the best findings from Black Hat and Defcon, from a hacked kids’ smartwatch to a coin-sized device that can hijack a Boeing 737.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

  • The Rise of the 1 am Job Interview
  • Hackers Stalked Me by Hijacking a Smartwatch for Kids
  • This Coin-Sized Device Can Hack a Boeing 737
  • McDonald’s Built a 515-Page Dossier on Me. It Says I’ll Never Stop Eating There

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger, and Andy Greenberg on Bluesky at @agreenberg. Write to us at [email protected].

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “Uncanny Valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Transcript

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Leah, how did you like The Odyssey?

Leah Feiger: I liked it.

Brian Barrett: Good.

Leah Feiger: I really liked it. I thought it was fun. The dialog was kind of whatever, beautiful shots of the Sicilian ocean. And I went with my husband who loves to remind me that he studied Latin and Greek in high school, and he actually liked it too. So frankly, 10 out of 10 from our family.

Brian Barrett: Good. Yeah, I agree. I think everyone who is complaining about it needs to stop. Anyway, welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I am Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Brian Barrett: Today on the show, we're going to be talking about Mark Zuckerberg's manifesto on AI, which weighs in at over 6,500 words. We will be talking about it for less time than it would take to read it, so you're welcome for that. But most importantly, we'll discuss what it says about Meta's strategy as it continuously tries to catch up in the AI race.

Leah Feiger: We'll also get into the rise of the 1 am job interview. As more people talk to a bot instead of a human for their first interview rounds, some job seekers are choosing to schedule theirs very late at night. We're going to look into that and how it's far from the only way that AI is changing job interviews as we know them.

Brian Barrett: And later in the show, we'll be joined by WIRED's Andy Greenberg to dive into some of the most exciting research that came out of Black Hat and Defcon, two of the world's biggest cybersecurity events. So on Monday, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg published a roughly 6,500-word essay on AI titled "The Future Is for Everyone." And doesn't that sound nice? It's the latest entry in the unfortunate genre of philosophical manifestos from tech CEOs. They've all got one. Sam Altman, Dario Amodei. Everyone's got a manifesto these days.

Leah Feiger: It's a requirement.

Brian Barrett: Some people have multiple manifestos. Even Zuckerberg's manifesto was an expansion of a Wall Street Journal op-ed that he wrote. Anyway, they all want to lay out their views for the industry, for the world, why their companies are best positioned to tackle the future, why you shouldn't be scared of their products, right? The core argument of Zuckerberg's manifesto is that concentrating AI power in a few institutions is dangerous, and broad access to these models is what you need to diffuse that power. He didn't name specific names, clearly taking jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, which favor tighter control over their private models. At one point he writes, and I quote, "Historically hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes."

Leah Feiger: I think it's a pretty Philosophy 101 way to say I just wasn't invited to play at the sandbox with the big kids. I mean, we can't divorce this from Meta's desperate attempts to stay relevant in the AI industry and race. And also we have to talk about the fact that they laid off so many people on this team just a few months ago. It was so all over the place. So there's something very funny to me about Mark Zuckerberg being like, "Whoa, whoa, whoa, let's rein in OpenAI and Anthropic." But I'm like, "You wish that you were them. That feels very obvious."

Brian Barrett: I wanted to get on that a little bit, Leah, too, in terms of the layoffs you mentioned and Meta's overall AI strategy, which has been so all over the place. They were all in for the longest time on open-source, open-weight models, because that was a way to counteract and undercut people who were trying to more directly profit off of closed models, OpenAI, Anthropic. That wasn't working. So they spent billions of dollars on this massive hiring spree to create this superintelligence lab that has not produced anything that has caught up to where the bigger labs are yet. So now he's saying, actually, maybe open is better, right? It's like when you can't win a race and so you say, "Actually, we shouldn't be racing at all. This race is dumb. Why aren't we just all sharing everything?" The other thing about this manifesto we haven't talked about yet is—and God, I hate that we call it that. Like manifesto makes it sound—

Leah Feiger: I hate it. I really—

Brian Barrett: It's marketing. What his marketing screed said, it's very "Hey everybody, don't worry. AI's just fine and it's going to be great for you. Why is everybody so upset about all this stuff? Don't you trust us to make your life better?" And this is coming from Meta, a company that I just have to say a week ago-ish, not even, was ordered by a court to pay $567 million for failing to do enough to protect kids' mental health online. Why are we trusting Meta with anything, much less AI and its impacts on society?

Leah Feiger: 100 percent. I also just can't help but think about almost like last summer when the massive hiring spree and competition was going on between OpenAI's and Meta's superintelligence labs, the insane salaries and competition. And again, it just felt like we're just grabbing. We're grabbing onto the hottest, flashiest thing, even if we don't have the systems backing it up right now. And especially Meta just announced a new open-weight system called Muse Glimmer on Monday, where users are able to download and alter the model as they wish. It's a lot of pivoting. I will be totally honest with you, I skimmed this manifesto. I read it. I for sure maybe read it in the background of a call, but I read it and it was a lot of nothing. It was a lot of nothing to me. But I know that Zoë had a lot of thoughts on it. She's not here with us today, but she did want to share some things.

Zoë Schiffer: OK. So first off, I think it's worth asking why Mark Zuckerberg felt the need to write 6,500 words on his vision for AI superintelligence. He told reporter Alex Heath that it's because Meta is about to start releasing super-smart models, and he wants the world to basically understand his philosophy before that happens. I personally think it's because AI is super unpopular right now, and Meta has the opportunity, at least it believes it has the opportunity, to start turning the tide, I guess, and also to position itself as better than its rivals, whom everyone currently seems to hate. The problem in my mind is that this manifesto doesn't seem to take AI all that seriously. Mark Zuckerberg uses the example of an agent creating personalized recipes so that he and his daughter can bake together. And I guess that sounds sweet, although aside from the fact of why do you need a personalized cookie recipe? It just seems to fundamentally miss the fact that these tools are dangerous. They're powerful, and we need AI leaders and tech leaders who take that danger really seriously.

Brian Barrett: If Zoë were here, and I'm sorry she’s not, but I’m glad she shared that. I would also be celebrating with her the fact that, however many months into this podcast, Leah, we got you to name-drop a specific AI model.

Leah Feiger: Gross.

Brian Barrett: And say what it does. Incredible how far you've come and how far we've dragged you into this muck. But no, I think her point is exactly right. It's this very breezy description of AI and how everybody's going to have a job, and your job's going to be easy, and you can have time with your daughter and make recipes and dah, dah, dah. It does ignore, almost aggressively ignore, all the potential downsides that we've been seeing play out, especially over the last couple of weeks. We're in the summer of rogue AI agents, right? Including one of Meta's, and showing how unpredictable and out of control these things can be.

Leah Feiger: I mean, from the Trump White House, which has historically been so anti-AI-regulation that its very own AI czar for the first year of the Trump presidency, David Sacks, was like, "We're not regulating," to now where the White House has a slightly toothless, but still there, policy of sorts, especially in response to all these national security threats, hacking threats, et cetera. Clearly no one, no matter how AI celebratory or positive you are, can't even remotely pretend right now that you don't have to take these things seriously, and it's not just going to solve child care or what have you and teach your kid how to cook. That's not it anymore.

Brian Barrett: And if it were, would you even want it to be? Last note of this is that we did run this essay, whatever you want to call it, through Pangram, which is an AI detection tool that we trust for the most part. Human written, Leah.

Leah Feiger: I love that.

Brian Barrett: AI is good enough for recipes with his daughter, but not good enough to crank out a manifesto.

Leah Feiger: I think that's beautiful.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. OK. In other news, in other news, a delightful and maybe dystopian story from WIRED senior writer Kate Taylor. She published a story on a strange pattern that has been increasingly emerging. So here's the deal. So many first-round job interviews these days are done by AI. You sit down in front of a screen, and an AI interviewer asks you questions or prompts, or if it's not AI, it is a series of prompts that are programmed into software. And you just sort of answer that way and not get screened. You can do that literally anytime, because there's no human on the other end of it, so people who are looking for jobs are increasingly scheduling those interviews late at night, as late as 1 in the morning sometimes, Kate found, to get around any family calendar conflicts, work conflicts, the hassle of making up a dentist appointment when you're doing a job interview. Now people just sort of do it after the kids are in bed, sitting down in their living room, talking to an AI agent who's going to determine their livelihood.

Leah Feiger: I think you're going to be shocked by my take.

Brian Barrett: OK, I'm ready.

Leah Feiger: I like it.

Brian Barrett: Wah.

Leah Feiger: I like that this is flexible.

Brian Barrett: Which part of it?

Leah Feiger: OK. Historically, I'm that person who was honestly really, really bad at doctor's appointments and dentist appointments. Not because I was not interested in my health, but because I just couldn't figure out how to schedule it during my day. No, I did not want to go at noon. I'm busy. I have work. I have a life. The idea that things like this that perhaps you have to do, job interview, doctor's appointment, whatever it is, the idea that you can do it on your schedule, to me, I'm like, that's positive. That is one positive thing that I see coming out of all of this. And I get it. Look, do I think that automation for job interviews is really what I'm looking for right now? Absolutely not. I think there's a lot of beautiful intricacies of the human experience and what people can bring to a workplace that cannot be captured adequately by a chatbot. However, if that is where society is right now, let it happen.

Brian Barrett: I'm impressed—or maybe not impressed, that might not be the right word—but I'm surprised by how many people are actually taking advantage of this. Kate talked to two different voice AI recruiting companies, one called Ribbon, one called Greenhouse. As many as a quarter, 15 to 25 percent of job candidates schedule between 10 pm and 2 am. I am not at my freshest at that moment, but I do think in some of these cases, you get to do as many takes, I guess, as you want of your response. You don't like how you responded. You can do it again until you send it in. I think that's how this works at least for some of these systems. So that's maybe another benefit that you have there. The downside, of course, is that AI also does the first review of all of these interviews. And so you are getting scored on your enthusiasm in some cases. You get an enthusiasm score for how do you turn up on camera. You're getting graded against a rubric that the hiring company sets. And the odds that a human actually will look at your tape and judge your response themselves are increasingly low. And that's the part that I think really gets to people.

Leah Feiger: No, that's horrible. You're absolutely right. The idea of someone looking at my résumé and being like, "Well, it didn't hit this one, two thing." You're like, "Well, we could have talked about that." That's difficult. That's less pleasant.

Brian Barrett: I know you like this in theory, and I get that. If you were applying for a job and they said, "OK, first round is with an AI interview, you're just going to answer some prompts and go from there." Would you take that as a sign to ditch the job process, or would you be like, "Alright, let's roll with it"?

Leah Feiger: I think it really depends, right? This is mentioned by Kate Taylor in the article. The economy is really not great for job seekers. The latest jobs report was absolutely horrific. The US economy lost something like 23,000 jobs in July. That's a not small number. So yeah, if I'm in a situation where I need work, absolutely. How do you say no to this?

Brian Barrett: Now Leah, hear me out. We are almost at a point. In fact, we are probably already there if you've got some savvy, which I know you do.

Leah Feiger: Thanks, Brian.

Brian Barrett: No, it's true. People should know. You sign up for an AI job interview. Instead of you sitting down, you set up a deepfake of yourself. Get Claude Code or something, plug it into an AI agent or a chatbot and have it give perfect responses to every question they throw your way. People already use AI to write their cover letters.

Leah Feiger: Robots interviewing robots.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. So it's robots interviewing robots all the way down, and may the best robot win.

Leah Feiger: So can we move on to talk about some cybersecurity news?

Brian Barrett: People may know that I used to be WIRED’s security editor, so I love to talk about security news.

Leah Feiger: Famously loves security. You heard it here first. OK. Last week, the Black Hat and Defcon conferences took place in Las Vegas. These are some of the world's largest and most respected annual cybersecurity events. Every summer, they bring together thousands of security professionals, hackers, government agencies, and general hacking aficionados to share cutting-edge security research and trends. WIRED's Andy Greenberg followed the research being released in real time and is now joining to tell us all about it. Hey, Andy.

Andy Greenberg: Hey everyone. Glad to be here. I can attest that Brian was in fact my editor on the security beat.

Leah Feiger: Was he good? You can tell me the truth.

Andy Greenberg: He was fantastic.

Brian Barrett: Look at that.

Andy Greenberg: He also wrote more than me, which was embarrassing.

Brian Barrett: But not nearly as well is the key.

Andy Greenberg: That's also debatable.

Leah Feiger: I want to jump right in. As the one non-security professional on this call, I have so many questions about the Black Hat conference. Every single year, I feel like I look at this in shock, in awe, in terror. In the AI era, I actually can't even really imagine what it was like as all of this is dropping at the same time. Maybe give it to me straight. What are the most dangerous hacking techniques that came out of this conference? What were the really big takeaways that people were talking about?

Andy Greenberg: Well, I do sometimes wonder what it's like to be a layperson reading all of this news that comes out of these two Las Vegas conferences, Black Hat and Defcon, every year.

Leah Feiger: Scary. I can tell you. Scary.

Andy Greenberg: Yeah. It creates a lot of very scary headlines, but these are generally what we call white-hat hackers or at least gray-hat hackers who are trying to demonstrate hacking techniques to get them fixed. And I think that's with AI too, that's an incredibly important thing to keep in mind. AI is an incredible bug hunting tool. In fact, like an exploit-building tool. It can build hacking techniques that humans can't build as quickly or at all. But the people doing this, for the most part, especially with the most powerful tools like Mythos for instance, are doing it generally to find vulnerabilities and get them fixed. And that's happening at these conferences too, for the most part.

Brian Barrett: Andy, you are great at doing experiential security reporting, by which I mean you're great at letting security researchers hack your things and put you in compromising positions. One of my favorite stories out of these conferences that you did this year, you let a group of researchers track you, eavesdrop on you, take pictures of you while you were wearing an adorable pink children's smartwatch. Can you tell us a little bit about that?

Andy Greenberg: Yes, that is all correct, but that wasn't honestly the plan for this story. So these two researchers who are presenting at Black Hat, Vangelis Stykas and Felipe Solferini, had found vulnerabilities in dozens, in fact, of GPS-enabled devices, including smartwatches for kids. And they were planning to present this. And in fact, what they wanted to highlight was that really just three Chinese companies serve as the kind of backends for dozens and dozens of these cheap GPS gadgets. And all of them, all three of those Chinese platforms, had really serious security vulnerabilities. So a parent might buy a SafeKid smartwatch in Sweden, and then some other parent in Spain might buy their SaveFamily watch, these different brands of smart watches for kids. But all of them are hosted essentially on the same Alibaba cloud backend in mainland China, and in fact have the same security vulnerabilities that leave those kids, those devices open to tracking. And to demonstrate this, the researchers just suggested that they ship me one of these watches, that they buy it off Amazon and ship it to me. And I said, OK, and received it, set it up, and they immediately showed that they could track my every move and even listen in on my conversations through this watch and secretly take photos of me. So this stalking experiment was not actually the initial idea of the story, but it really drove home the vulnerability of these cheap devices.

Leah Feiger: And these researchers aren't usually just focused on things like this, right? At least one of them spent a really long time studying North Korean hackers. You had reported that they actually found that these hackers have breached hundreds of networks over the years. These are people very entrenched in all of this.

Andy Greenberg: That's right. Vangelis Stykas actually was presenting two talks at Black Hat. And the other one was about years of work that he's done actually penetrating the infrastructure of North Korean hackers. And he was revealing for the first time that he had gotten into their servers and sort of hacked the hackers, and then was able to find evidence of all of the hundreds of companies these North Korean hackers have themselves penetrated. I should say that the North Korean hackers were really focused on stealing cryptocurrency as they do. So some of the data that they accessed was probably not even that interesting to them, but they did, for instance, hack a hospital and get access to Covid data on practically every American. In another case, Vangelis found that they had hacked into a company that had criminal records of every American who has a criminal record. So these are extremely sensitive troves of data that North Koreans were getting access to just in the process of really kind of casting a very wide net, breaching tons of companies, mostly for financial gain.

Brian Barrett: We have a ton of great coverage from Black Hat and Defcon, including some wild stuff about OpenAI and their rogue agents and how all of it happened sort of under their noses. Some other stories from Matt Burgess and Lily Hay Newman. But I want to talk, Andy, too, about another story that happened just after Black Hat and Defcon, more of an academic conference where you found some cybersecurity research, including how a tiny coin-sized device could hack a Boeing 737 if you have just 60 seconds of access to the exterior of the plane.

Andy Greenberg: So there's actually a third conference in this series, Black Hat, Defcon, and then this other one, USENIX, which is an academic conference, as you said. Most people kind of, I think, ignore this one, but some of the most interesting research is coming out of academia, in fact. And this was a group of researchers at UC San Diego and Oberlin College who spent more than 10 years trying to hack a plane. In fact, some of these researchers were the first to hack cars over the internet in the early 2010s. And they moved onto planes and wanted to see if it's possible to hack a plane again, to find vulnerabilities to warn the aviation industry, to get ahead of somebody who would actually want to do this and cause harm. And ultimately, after years of work and tens of thousands of dollars of purchases of plane components, they found that they could in fact hack a Boeing 737 if they can get about 60 seconds of physical access to the exterior of the plane. They can open a hatch and put in this little device that they built that's about the size of a coin, plug it into this one specific port. And using that little device, they can change the navigation of the plane's autopilots. They can rewrite its flight plan. They can mess with the numbers that go into the calculation of its takeoff speed, like the plane's weight and the outside air temperature, very scary stuff. But again, with the goal of warning Boeing about this vulnerability before somebody can actually take advantage of it.

Leah Feiger: Lot of conferences, lot of lessons learned, lot of fear for me personally. Were there any surprises for you? You're so mired in this world. What stayed with you here?

Andy Greenberg: Actually, Lily was the one who was most on the ground in Black Hat and at Defcon, and who did the majority of the coverage of all of the advances in AI hacking, as you were talking about at the top of this. And what surprised me, both in her reporting and my own conversations at the conference is not really the power of AI, but some of its limitations in terms of finding vulnerabilities and hacking techniques. So Lilly wrote a great story about one researcher who was showing the ways in which actually AI has blind spots where it will hit a dead end without a human hacker assisting it. And in fact, humans and AI together is kind of this like, that's the recipe that adds up to really novel hacking techniques. I heard from some really sophisticated hackers that AI, yes, is finding incredible new vulnerabilities in zero days in all kinds of systems, but that there are certain kinds of exploits that it cannot find still because it's trained on hackers' prior work. Like all AI, it's trained on training data. If it's never seen a whole class of attack, it won't be able to carry that out itself. So I think the lesson that I took away from Black Hat and Defcon is really that, like a lot of artificial intelligence from the past applied to things like chess or Go or whatever, the most powerful combination is humans and AI working together, and that really will start to create and hopefully patch vulnerabilities we've never seen before.

Brian Barrett: Yeah, let's get the patching in there first, if possible.

Andy Greenberg: At least before something bad happens, yes.

Brian Barrett: Andy, thank you so much for joining us today. Always a real treat to talk to you.

Andy Greenberg: Well, thank you both for talking about all this.

Brian Barrett: Coming up after the break, we'll share our WIRED/TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us.

Leah Feiger: OK. It is time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. Whatever is new and cool is WIRED. Whatever passé thing we're over is TIRED. Brian, what do you got?

Brian Barrett: Leah Feiger, my WIRED is a #3 extra value meal from McDonald's. It's the classic. You've got a Quarter Pounder with cheese, medium fries, medium drink. I go with Coke Zero, but whatever you prefer. That's WIRED. TIRED is the amount of data that McDonald's collects from anyone who uses their app. WIRED senior writer Reece Rogers this week had a really, really great story where he took advantage of the fact that in California he's got a legal right to access any data that a company stores about him. So he sent a request off to McDonald's and came back with a 515-page file in his inbox of everything that McDonald's knows about him.

Leah Feiger: Unreal.

Brian Barrett: It's incredible. Some of the things that McDonald's tracks, it's not just what they … So there's the stuff that you would assume, like how much he has spent and what his order history is, and even some location history stuff. And to be clear, Reece uses the McDonald's app, which is where a lot of this is coming from. So if you just go into a store and pay with a credit card, it's going to look a lot different. But not only that, McDonald's has predictive things about Reece. They estimate the number of visits he'll take over the next six weeks, apparently 2.16. They'll estimate his average order spend during the next six weeks, $13.49. They estimate his consumer attrition likelihood, how likely it is that he'll stop being a McDonald's customer at some point. Reese scored a zero on that. They've got him for life. And my favorite, Leah, my favorite part of this, as much as you can have a favorite part of a fast food Panopticon, they've ranked the 10 McDonald's products most relevant to him. The top three in order are large Diet Coke. OK. Spicy Snack Wrap, sure. And number three, the Grinch McShaker fry, large.

Leah Feiger: That's so good.

Brian Barrett: So that's my TIRED.

Leah Feiger: That's incredible stuff. If anyone listening to us has not read Reece's article yet, I highly recommend it. I would put it in the class of old school blogs, AKA endless mozzarella cheese sticks at TGI Fridays. It's in that genre for me. It's excellent.

Brian Barrett: Yep. It's terrific. Now, Leah, what is your WIRED/TIRED this week?

Leah Feiger: My WIRED is that it is currently humpback whale season across many parts of the world. In French Polynesia, in Australia's Ningaloo Reef. There are humpback whales and their young making their way.

Brian Barrett: Ooh.

Leah Feiger: I love to see it. The videos online are inspiring. And just with everything happening, it's nice to know that there's this return. There's this seasonal shift. I've been harboring these fears following a lot of our El Niño coverage, which has been excellent. Go check out the science section on WIRED.com of just what that would do to all of these migration patterns. And all to say that they could still be very much affected in the next year. It has been very nice to see that not happening, at least right in this moment. That is my WIRED.

Brian Barrett: It's a beautiful thing, and it makes me terrified about what your TIRED is about to be.

Leah Feiger: My TIRED is there was an article a couple of days ago that's been going around my community about how a number of Antarctic tour guides have been quitting their jobs after witnessing tourism's major damage to the continent—things getting left behind and the impact on penguin populations. Really sad. And I'm very obsessed with Antarctica, as you know. So this is ocean-related, sea-related. Everyone's coming in via ocean. And it's been really interesting. I actually went to Antarctica a couple of years ago. It was an unbelievable experience. You had to do a crossing. You had to do the Drake Passage. Now tourists are getting flown in and out, which is an entirely new thing. And building runways across the continent, there's been all of these studies about them disrupting penguin migrations and all sorts of other things. And it's been really sad to witness this. So then a couple days ago when it came out that all these guides were actually quitting their jobs over this, it's been kind of sobering, like, it's amazing that the world is so open and available, and it's also so scary that the natural world is so open and available. It is a sobering moment to go like, "Oh God, what have we done to these beautiful places?" Something I'm sitting with right now.

Brian Barrett: So any Uncanny Valley listeners who are lucky enough to go to Antarctica, be cool.

Leah Feiger: Be cool.

Brian Barrett: I think is our message.

Leah Feiger: Be cool.

Brian Barrett: Be cool. Just be cool.

Leah Feiger: Be cool about it.

Brian Barrett: Just be cool.

Zoë Schiffer: That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

entries.title: The Painful Truth of Exactly How ICE’s New Shock Gloves Work
entries.summary: ICE is spending millions on shock gloves designed to overpower subjects through intense, localized pain.
entries.content:
With the revelation that ICE will spend up to $20 million by March on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to subdue an individual, according to a notice published earlier this week by the Department of Homeland Security, it's worth looking at how this apparel, designated as a nonlethal tool for law enforcement, actually works.

These shock gloves go by the unsubtle acronym of GLOVE (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter) and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies, based in Lexington, Kentucky. The GLOVE, previously used in jails and police departments in the US, looks and functions like a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate an electrical mode.

Classified as a CD3 (conductive distraction and de-escalation device), the gloves don't work like stun guns or Tasers, which shoot out probes or use high voltages to cause neuromuscular incapacitation that overrides the central nervous system. Instead, the GLOVE works using neuro-peripheral interference, essentially shocking the skin to bombard the sensory nerves and temporarily short-circuit the brain's focus.

Compliant Technologies did not respond to WIRED's request for comment.

When activated via a one-second press on a wrist switch, conductive pads embedded on the palm and undersides of the fingers of the gloves can transmit high-frequency electrical pulses directly to the wearer’s point of contact on a subject. A rechargeable battery and microprocessor module tucked inside a zippered pouch on the cuff powers the entire system.

The electrical pulse overstimulates nerve endings in the subject's peripheral nervous system, resulting in pain that inhibits coordinated muscle movement, but without causing systemic muscle lockup. The pain induced is localized to just the area touched by the glove's conductive pads. The manufacturer claims the gloves result in a subject's compliance in less than three seconds and leave no burns, marks, or scars.

Because the current flows only between the contact pads on the device and across the subject's skin, the officer wearing the GLOVE, as well as any assisting officers holding the subject, should not feel electrical shocks. The gloves, capable of operating between 14 and 122 degrees Fahrenheit, come in three versions: Gen 3, 4, and 5. Maximum voltage is capped at 380 V for all, and the minimum voltage for Gen 3 and 4 is 210 V, which rises to 324 V for Gen 5.

Maximum stimulation time on Gen 3 and 4 models is a sobering two hours, though that drops to 90 minutes for Gen 5. The battery is apparently good for 2,000 charge/discharge cycles, and it can recharge to full in two hours. Four LED lights on the gloves display the current charge level, each noting 25 percent battery increments.

Gen 4 and 5 of GLOVE both include mechanisms that record “activation events,” tracking the date, hour, minute, and skin-contact time for audit trails and after-action reporting. Gen 4 stores this data on a removable microSD card, while Gen 5 does away with this in favor of built-in internal memory, accessed via a USB-C cable.

There's a test function on the gloves, too, where operators can verify they are working by tapping an active pad against their own forearm to feel a minor electrical pulse. According to the manuals, GLOVE users must be certified and then recertified every other year to continue using the device.

GLOVE, which can only be sold to verified professional entities such as the military, correctional facilities, and law enforcement agencies—has some clear usage recommendations in Compliant Technologies' instruction manuals:

  • No more than two GLOVE units (or, in other words, one pair) should be used simultaneously on a single subject.
  • Continuous shocks should not exceed 15 seconds.
  • Operators must target arms and legs, while strictly avoiding the head, face, throat, chest, and groin.
  • The gloves should not be used on the elderly, young children, pregnant individuals, or people with severe disabilities.
  • The technology must not be used to counter verbal defiance, as punishment, or for torture.

Crucially, the GLOVE has limitations, chief among them that for the device to work effectively and deliver its restraining pain shock, it must come into contact with the subject's bare skin. According to Compliant Technologies, the gloves won't work through dry clothing or thick hair. The gloves will work, however, if the subject is wearing thin, wet clothing, such as soaked T-shirts or blouses. The GLOVE also does not like being dunked in water and will likely be rendered inoperable if this happens.

Michael Crowley, a senior researcher at Omega Research Foundation—an organization that tracks human rights abuses committed across the world by people using police, security, and military equipment—is concerned that the GLOVE is seemingly designed not to restrain or incapacitate, but to hurt.

“CD3 technology inflicts pain," Crowley says. "The company talks about it as a de-escalation solution, but the whole idea of it is to get control or influence somebody through pain. Omega considers it to be an inherently abusive technology that should not be manufactured, sold, or used by law enforcement officials, including ICE.”
